firstLine: November travel feels like a quiet reward after the year’s rush.
"November is the month for destinations that feel like a warm embrace after the year’s chill.
Planning a trip with friends can feel like handing over your privacy to every app you use.
text:
Planning a trip with friends can feel like handing over your privacy to every app you use. 

We built Roamie so that the only data it keeps is what’s needed for the trip itself. No profiling, no trackers, no hidden details about who you are beyond what you share. 

That means no ads following you, no third parties guessing your habits, nothing stored beyond the votes, the wheel spins, and the destination chosen. It’s just a tool for deciding where to go, and nothing more. 

We don’t ask for much in return. What would you trust a tool to keep private when planning a trip?

firstLine: Planning a trip with friends often means coordinating messages, spreadsheets, and endless back-and-forth.
text:
Planning a trip with friends often means coordinating messages, spreadsheets, and endless back-and-forth. 

We built Roamie to make that easier. Anyone can join a trip with a link or a short code, no app to download, nothing to sign up for. It’s just a page in the browser, and it stays free. 

The goal was to keep it simple: no extra steps, no friction. If you’ve ever wasted time trying to get everyone on the same page, you’ll know why that matters. 

What’s the one thing that always slows down your group’s planning?

firstLine: This week’s small steps make Roamie a little more reliable for the trips that matter most.
text:
This week’s small steps make Roamie a little more reliable for the trips that matter most.

We fixed a few things that might have caused frustration when sharing a trip. If you’ve ever tried to add a video and it didn’t work, it should now. If a post looked the same two days in a row, that won’t happen again. And if you’ve ever lost track of a draft on TikTok, you’ll see where it got to before it disappeared.

The landing page now shows photos with the guide cards, so you can picture the kind of trips people are planning. And if you’ve ever wondered why a post didn’t go through, you’ll see the attempts we tried and discarded, so you know we’re not giving up.

What’s the one thing that still makes planning a trip feel like too much work?

firstLine: Deciding where to go isn’t just about counting votes. It’s about the reasons behind them.
text:
Deciding where to go isn’t just about counting votes. It’s about the reasons behind them.

When someone says they’d like to go because of a cheap flight or a friend who lives nearby, it carries more weight than just a yes or no. A good reason can shift opinions without anyone feeling left out. It turns a simple choice into something more thoughtful.

That’s why the best trips often start with a conversation, not just a tally. Sometimes the most persuasive argument isn’t the loudest one.

What’s the last trip you convinced a friend to join, and what made it convincing?

firstLine: A city where the night stays alive but the day offers quiet warmth.
text:
A city where the night stays alive but the day offers quiet warmth. 

Bucharest’s old town is packed with bars that spill into the streets after dark, while a short trip away brings Therme, a sprawling spa where the only thing you’ll be racing is the steam. It’s the kind of balance that works for a group who want to stay up late but still need somewhere to recover the next morning. 

The city is easy on the budget too, which means you could stretch the trip further, maybe with a day trip to explore the countryside or just more time in the bars and pools. It’s not the kind of place that demands a strict itinerary, which can be a relief when you’re planning with friends. 

Does your group need a mix of energy and rest, or do you prefer destinations that lean one way or the other?

firstLine: We didn’t realise how much language could slow down a group trip until we saw it happen. Sometimes the easiest way to decide isn’t the fastest.
text:
We didn’t realise how much language could slow down a group trip until we saw it happen. Sometimes the easiest way to decide isn’t the fastest.

A conversation about a trip can get stuck when everyone speaks different languages. Maybe one person suggests a place, another replies in their own language, and the rest don’t understand. Or maybe someone shares a link, and it gets lost in translation. By the time everyone’s caught up, the momentum is gone.

We built Roamie so the app would handle the language barrier for you. Every suggestion, vote, and comment stays in the language it was written, but the app translates it for everyone else. No one gets left out, and no one has to pause to ask what was said.

It’s not about making decisions faster, it’s about making sure no one feels left behind when the conversation moves on.

How often do language differences slow down your group’s plans?

firstLine: The moment you assume everyone shares your excitement for a trip is the moment it starts to unravel.
text:
The moment you assume everyone shares your excitement for a trip is the moment it starts to unravel.

There’s a quiet tension in many group trips: the person who spent hours researching flights and activities, only to be met with half-hearted replies. Or the one who’s already counting down the days, while others are still debating whether to go at all. It’s not that enthusiasm is the problem, it’s the mismatch between what you assume and what’s actually there.

The trip isn’t just about the destination. It’s about the energy of the people in it. If one person is dragging their feet, or another feels unheard, the whole experience shifts. The best trips don’t just balance excitement, they balance effort, too. Someone might not be as hyped as you, but they could be the one who keeps things running smoothly. Someone else might seem disengaged, but they could be the reason the group stays together at all.

How do you talk about the trip without letting the planning become another source of frustration?

firstLine: We used to assume speed was the same everywhere. It wasn’t.
text:
We used to assume speed was the same everywhere. It wasn’t.

When we tested features on our laptops, they felt instant. But on a mid-range phone, even small interactions could stutter. We learned the hard way that what works for one device doesn’t work for all.

Now, we simulate a mid-range phone before every release. We slow the processor, measure the lag, and fix it before users notice. It’s a small habit, but it saved us from shipping half-measures.

How often do you test on the devices your users actually have?

firstLine: A trip that doesn’t need a packed itinerary.
text:
A trip that doesn’t need a packed itinerary. 

The Dolomites offer a different kind of adventure. Instead of rushing from one place to another, there’s time to pause at mountain huts for lunch, where the views of Seceda or Tre Cime di Lavaredo unfold slowly over a shared meal. The trails here suit everyone, from those who want a steady climb to those who prefer a gentler walk. 

Val Gardena and Alta Badia make good bases for a group. They’re close enough to explore without feeling scattered, with enough small villages and quiet spots to unwind between hikes. It’s the kind of place where the trip feels light, even when the budget isn’t extravagant. 

We’ve seen groups here who came for the scenery but stayed for the rhythm, no need to fill every hour. It’s not about doing everything, but about the moments that stick. 

What’s the one place you’d revisit just to slow down?

firstLine: The way people use Roamie changes how it feels.
text:
The way people use Roamie changes how it feels.

This week, we made the first step simpler. The screen you see when you open Roamie now starts with a clear action: proposing a place. The old button that asked you to paste a group chat link is gone. It was never the right way to begin.

The map looks different too. On wide screens, the grey strip above the poles is gone, replaced by the same filtered sea colour as the rest of the world. The wheel has changed as well, trading its bright rim lights for a softer sunset dial and a compass bezel. It’s more like a quiet moment of decision than a game.

Small text is easier to read now. The smallest size has grown, and the labels on the landing page, ticket prices, country names, photo credits, the invite note, have moved up to match. The scroll story on the landing page also zooms into the postcard the hero wheel picks, making the connection between the decision and the destination clearer.

We’re still working on a few things behind the scenes, like a simpler way to sign in. For now, we’ve made the steps you take every day a little more direct.

What’s the one thing that still feels awkward when you use Roamie?

firstLine: Money complicates trips more than most of us admit.
text:
Money complicates trips more than most of us admit.

The conversation about who’s paying for what often starts with silence. Someone assumes others will cover flights, another expects meals to be split evenly, and no one mentions it until the receipts arrive. By then, the trip has already become a source of tension, not just a shared memory.

It’s not about who pays more or less. It’s about avoiding the moment when a friendly group turns into a room of people calculating who owes what. That silence, the one where no one wants to bring up money, is where the real problem begins.

How do you and your friends handle trip costs before the first expense comes up?
x: Money questions before the trip save friendships after it. Who’s paying for flights, who’s splitting meals, who’s bringing the snacks. The silence around these details is where the awkwardness starts. Better to clarify early than argue after the Uber ride.

firstLine: Pizza, coffee and alleys where Vesuvius watches over the city.
text:
Pizza, coffee and alleys where Vesuvius watches over the city. 

Naples has a way of making food feel like a shared ritual. The cafés stay busy long after dinner, and every corner offers something that tastes like it’s been perfected over generations. It’s the kind of place where you don’t need a plan, just an appetite and the willingness to wander. 

If the group splits between history and scenery, an extra day could take you to Pompeii’s quiet streets or the quiet charm of Procida. Both are close enough to keep the trip simple, without the rush of a longer journey. 

It’s one of those destinations where the budget stretches further than you’d expect. The real cost is in the time you’ll spend deciding what to try next. 

Have you been somewhere where the food alone made the trip feel worth it?
x: Naples lets you fill a trip with pizza, coffee and wandering alleys without overthinking the plan. The budget lasts longer than the indecision over what to eat next.

firstLine: The first idea in a group doesn’t always belong to the person who had it longest. Sometimes it’s just the one who spoke up first.
text:
The first idea in a group doesn’t always belong to the person who had it longest. Sometimes it’s just the one who spoke up first.

There’s a quiet cost to letting opinions settle around whoever starts the conversation. The loudest voice rarely represents the group’s actual balance of enthusiasm, memory or practicality. It’s just who happened to go first.

When decisions are made in silence, before anyone else speaks, the group gets closer to what it truly wants. That’s when the quieter voices, who might have held back out of habit or hesitation, finally share what matters to them.

We’ve seen it happen in small ways: a suggestion that wouldn’t have surfaced otherwise, a preference that changes the whole direction. It’s not about fairness in the strictest sense. It’s about giving the conversation room to breathe before it’s over.

How often do you realise, after the fact, that the trip you ended up taking wasn’t the one the group actually wanted?
x: The first idea isn’t always the best one. It’s often just the first one spoken. Quieter voices matter just as much. Let everyone vote first, before the loudest opinion takes over.

firstLine: Some trips feel like a race to see everything. Others are about lingering.
text:
Some trips feel like a race to see everything. Others are about lingering.

November brings destinations where the pace slows naturally. In Istanbul, the bazaars and mosques hold their own weight, while the Bosphorus ferries glide past without haste. The bars in Karaköy stay open late, but the city doesn’t rush you. A month where history and food share the same tables, and the budget stretches further than the walk between them.

Marrakech in November means the square at Jemaa el-Fna settles into its evening rhythm, the riads feel like private retreats, and the desert or mountains don’t demand a full day’s attention. It’s a place where the trip unfolds in layers, some chosen, some discovered along the way.

Cappadocia in late autumn turns the fairy chimneys into something softer, the cave hotels into cosy nooks, and the valleys into quiet spaces where snow lingers. The hot-air balloons still rise at dawn, but the rest of the day belongs to whoever wants to stay in or wander without a plan.

What’s the kind of trip your group needs most right now, the one that feels like a checklist, or the one that feels like a pause?
x: November’s best for trips that slow down. Istanbul’s bazaars and Bosphorus ferries let you linger. Marrakech’s riads and desert trips unfold at your own pace. Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys and cave hotels feel like a quiet pause. Where’s your group’s next pause needed most?

firstLine: We thought we knew what people needed until we saw how they actually used the app.
text:
We thought we knew what people needed until we saw how they actually used the app.

Our first version had a way to add destinations, vote and pick one. It worked, but it didn’t quite fit how groups really decided. The best changes, like letting people add ideas without voting first or adjusting how the wheel worked, came from watching real conversations unfold. We didn’t notice these things ourselves.

The quiet feedback mattered more than our own assumptions. A few sentences from someone testing it could reveal what wasn’t obvious in our own minds. It’s easy to assume you understand how people will use something, but the details often surprise you.

What’s something you’ve built that only made sense after seeing real people use it?
x: We assumed we knew what people needed. Turns out, the best fixes came from watching real groups use it. Like letting everyone add ideas before voting. Small notes from testers showed us what we missed. What’s one thing your product only learned after real use?

firstLine: A place where the day and night feel like different worlds.
text:
A place where the day and night feel like different worlds. 

The island starts quiet, with a long stretch of sand to walk along or just lie on. It’s easy to imagine days spent reading, napping or doing nothing much at all. Then, as evening comes, the village fills with music and conversation. No one has to decide what to do next, it just happens. 

Some trips need a plan. Others need a rhythm. This one does neither. It’s more about the shift from stillness to movement, from solitude to company, than about checking off sights. 

Have you ever gone somewhere where the pace of the place matched the mood of the group?
x: Ios lets your group drift between beach silence and village noise without planning. The island does the switching for you. Some trips need a schedule. This one just needs a rhythm.

firstLine: Some trips need a wheel more than others.
text:
Some trips need a wheel more than others.

We added a new wheel for Italian holidays, showing nearby places and how the long weekend falls this year. It’s there if it helps, and gone if it doesn’t.

After a spin, you’ll see the odds that were used to pick the winner. It’s a small thing, but it makes it clearer how the wheel works.

The checklist now shows flights and stays for the next seven days with one tap. We also brought back the budget labels that were accidentally lost a while ago.

You can now choose between Auto, Light or Dark theme for your profile. It applies instantly, and we’ve made sure the smallest text, like privacy notices, is still easy to read.

Do you ever find yourself overthinking the odds of a spin?
x: The wheel picks a destination. Now it shows the odds that made it happen. No mystery, just clarity. Sometimes that’s all it takes to move forward.

firstLine: Deciding a trip with friends isn’t about the destination. It’s about the way the conversation gets stuck.
text:
Deciding a trip with friends isn’t about the destination. It’s about the way the conversation gets stuck.

Group chats don’t help. A suggestion lands, then gets lost under replies about work or dinner plans. Someone mentions an idea again, but no one’s sure if it’s new or just brought up before. The decision drifts to next week, then the week after, until the energy fades.

The problem isn’t the back-and-forth. It’s that the options aren’t in one place. When they are, the conversation shifts. People can see what’s been suggested, react to it, and move forward without wondering if they’ve already agreed, or forgotten.

We’ve seen this happen enough to know it’s not about the tool. It’s about giving the conversation room to breathe.

What usually stops your group from settling on a plan?
x: Group chats bury trip ideas under new messages. The decision never lands because the options aren’t in one place. Put them there first. The conversation changes.

firstLine: A walk where the path unfolds alongside water, not on top of it.
text:
A walk where the path unfolds alongside water, not on top of it.

The levadas on this island are quiet, shaded by trees that stay green year-round. They wind through valleys and up to viewpoints where the sun rises over cliffs before the rest of the world wakes up. There’s no rush to choose a route, just a steady climb or descent, the sound of water beside you, and the occasional glimpse of a distant village.

It’s the kind of place where you’d pack a picnic and spend the afternoon sitting on a bench that overlooks the sea. Or where you’d rent a car and drive until you found a spot no one else had thought of. The weather stays mild enough that layers work in any season, and the budget lets you stay in guesthouses or small hotels without feeling like you’re skimping.

We’ve seen groups use Roamie to balance adventure with stillness, like hiking one day and then taking the next to read, nap, or just watch the light change over the water. It’s not a trip that demands a plan, just one that rewards being there.

Have you ever chosen a destination because of the way it made you want to slow down?
x: Levadas in Madeira let you walk beside water, not over it. The pace is set by the path, not the clock. Where do you need a trip that moves as slowly as it should?

firstLine: The hardest part of planning a trip is often the calendar. Not the flights, not the hotels, not even the activities. Just figuring out when everyone can go.
text:
The hardest part of planning a trip is often the calendar. Not the flights, not the hotels, not even the activities. Just figuring out when everyone can go.

We built a way to show who’s free on which days, so you can see at a glance when the group can realistically meet. No back-and-forth messages guessing availability, no one accidentally double-booking. Just the dates that work for everyone.

It’s not about picking the perfect moment, it’s about finding the one that doesn’t leave anyone out. Sometimes that’s a narrow window, sometimes a few weeks. Either way, Roamie shows it straight away.

The goal isn’t to force a consensus. It’s to make sure no one’s left wondering if they’ll actually get to go.

Do you usually end up picking dates by elimination, or does someone always drop out at the last minute?
x: Finding dates for a trip should never be a game of elimination. Roamie shows who’s free when, so the right window appears first time. No last-minute dropouts, no guesswork. Just the dates that work for everyone.

firstLine: December is when some places feel like nowhere else.
text:
December is when some places feel like nowhere else.

Livigno’s slopes are quieter in winter, the snow parks are open, and the après-ski stays lively. It’s also a duty-free zone, so fuel and shopping cost less than usual. A mid-range budget covers it well.

Prague’s old town looks like a storybook in December, and its beer is still some of Europe’s cheapest. The clubs are multi-storey and the city feels alive, even when it’s cold outside.

Tromsø’s fjords and whales are reliable this month, and the northern lights are at their best. The sun doesn’t rise for weeks, but the evenings have a different kind of energy, bars, cafés and a sense of adventure.

Which of these would you linger in the longest?
x: December turns Livigno into quiet slopes and open snow parks. Prague’s old town glows under lights, its beer still cheap. Tromsø’s fjords and northern lights need no daylight. Which of these stays with you after the trip?

firstLine: A tester noticed something we missed: smooth animations on a computer didn’t mean they’d feel the same on a phone.
text:
A tester noticed something we missed: smooth animations on a computer didn’t mean they’d feel the same on a phone. 

We assumed the issue was obvious. The new page loaded as it animated, and the phone struggled to keep up. The computer handled it easily, but the phone’s resources were stretched thin. We’d focused on the visuals without checking how the device would actually process them. 

The fix was simpler than we expected. We separated the two tasks: let the graphics chip handle the animation while the main processor built the page afterward. No one had told us to do this, we just measured the problem and adjusted. 

It’s easy to assume what feels right on one device will work on another. Small details like this can make a big difference to someone using your app. 

Have you encountered a difference between how something works on a desktop and how it feels on a phone?
x: A tester saw our page transitions stutter on their phone, even though they looked smooth on a computer. Turns out the phone was trying to load and animate the page at once. Now it separates the two. Small tweaks, big difference.

firstLine: A trip where the water is always close by, even if you don’t always see it.
text:
A trip where the water is always close by, even if you don’t always see it.

Some places are made for groups who want to spread out, some by boat, some on foot, some just sitting on a terrace. The islands here are small enough to explore in a day, but far enough from the mainland to feel like another world. You could spend mornings anchored in a bay, afternoons wandering the harbour, and evenings watching the sun set over the water.

The way people travel here changes with the light. By day, it’s quiet, the kind of place where conversations drift between the table and the waves. By night, it’s louder, with music spilling from bars that stay open until dawn. It’s not a trip for those who want to rush, but for those who want to linger where they are.

Sharing a boat with friends makes it easier to imagine staying longer than a few days. The cost per person drops when you split it, and there’s something about deciding together where to go next that turns a weekend into something that feels like a proper break.

Have you ever been somewhere that felt different in the evening than it did in the morning?
x: Boat trips to Hvar’s Pakleni islands split costs, turn a weekend into days. The same bay looks quiet by day, alive by night. Where do you want your group to feel like this?

firstLine: Some trips start with a single idea. Others begin with a conversation.
text:
Some trips start with a single idea. Others begin with a conversation.

This week, we made it clearer how holidays fall on the calendar. The long-weekend pages now show the date for this year’s holiday, and the sitemap lists a real last-modified date for most pages, helpful for search engines and anyone checking when something was last updated.

The landing page and all prerendered pages now include Twitter/X tags, and we’ve added a list of the main pages for search engines to crawl. The sample trip also got a little more realistic: you can now see how votes change in real time when demo friends join, and the steps are marked off as you go.

A few small tweaks from tester feedback: the wheel no longer removes the picked place from the running while it’s spinning, and Italian pages now offer English as a fallback if your browser’s language isn’t supported.

What’s the one thing that always helps when planning a trip with friends?
x: Planning a trip with friends often gets stuck in the back-and-forth of ‘when are you free?’. What if you saw the dates that work for everyone at once? No more guessing, no more last-minute changes. Just the right window.

firstLine: Most trips hinge on one person carrying the weight.
text:
Most trips hinge on one person carrying the weight.

They’re the ones who check calendars, send reminders, and juggle bookings while everyone else drifts in and out of the conversation. It’s not that they want to be in charge, it’s just that no one else steps in to share the load. The plan lives in their messages, their notes, their head, and when they finally share it, the response is often silence or a half-hearted ‘sounds good.’

The real friction isn’t the planning itself. It’s the moment the group realises they’ve all assumed someone else will handle it. By then, the dates are set, the bookings are made, and the person left holding the pieces is the one who feels stuck.

What if the burden wasn’t just on one person? What if the plan wasn’t something to be handed over, but something to be built together, where everyone could see what was left to do and step in when they could?

How do you usually handle the parts of a trip that no one wants to own?
x: One person usually ends up organising the whole trip. Dates, bookings, reminders, it all piles up on them. What if the plan was shared from the start, so no one had to wait for someone else to take over?

firstLine: The map shows where the conversation went wrong.
text:
The map shows where the conversation went wrong.

When a group plans a trip, ideas often pile up. One person suggests a city, another counters with a different one, and soon the list grows long and scattered. Deciding which to pick can feel like sorting through a stack of unread messages, no clear way to start, no obvious choice. 

Our map brings all those ideas together in one place. Every proposed destination sits next to the others, marked clearly so the group can see at a glance what’s been suggested, what’s been picked, and what’s already been visited. It’s not about picking the best idea right away. It’s about making sure nothing gets lost in the shuffle.

The map helps the conversation stay focused. Instead of debating the same few places over and over, the group can move forward, knowing where they’ve been and where they’re still considering going. It turns a messy list into something clearer, so the real discussion can begin.

Have you ever lost track of where a group was in planning a trip? What usually helps bring it back together?
x: The map shows where the conversation went wrong. Ideas pile up in messages, lost in the shuffle. Roamie gathers them all, proposed, picked, visited, in one place. No more sorting through noise. Just clarity.

firstLine: December trips have a quiet kind of magic. The kind that settles in over coffee or a glass of wine, when the details start to matter more than the grand plan.
text:
December trips have a quiet kind of magic. The kind that settles in over coffee or a glass of wine, when the details start to matter more than the grand plan.

A few places feel especially alive this month. The half-timbered houses of Alsace, lined with canals and strung with lights, or the flower-filled villages along the Wine Route. The Christmas markets there are some of the most atmospheric in Europe, but the food and the wine are just as worth the trip any time of year.

Budapest has a different kind of warmth. The historic baths are perfect for unwinding, and the ruin bars in the Jewish Quarter have a lively energy that carries through December. The city stays affordable too, making it easy to linger over good food and a few nights out.

Kraków balances history and energy well. The medieval square is a place to walk slowly, while the Kazimierz district offers bars where conversations can stretch late into the evening. There’s also the Wieliczka salt mine, a unique stop that’s easy to add on.

Which of these would fit best with the kind of trip you’re imagining?
x: December trips have their own rhythm. Colmar’s canals glow with lights, Alsace’s wine route hums with quiet charm. Budapest’s baths steam while ruin bars pulse. Kraków’s square feels like a storybook, its bars full of late-night talk. Where do you want to linger?
